items.text: administrative warrants because administrative warrants raise serious constitutional concerns and directly affect the residents of our city. This issue is not abstract and it's not partisan. It goes to the heart of the Fourth Amendment in the relationship between local communities and government authority. The Fourth Amendment guarantees that people are secure in their homes and that the government may not search or seize without a warrant issued by an independent impartial judge based on probable cause. That safeguard exists for one reason to ensure that no government agency can act as judge and enforcer at the same time. Administrative warrants violate that principle. Unlike judicial warrants, administrative warrants are issued internally by government agencies. Remember, a municipal judge is appointed

items.title: city council · January 26, 2026 · 00:06:45
items.text: by the mayor and the council. Administrative warrants are not reviewed or approved by an independent judge. When an agency authorizes its enforcement actions, the constitutional check designed to protect the public is removed. That is exactly the kind of unchecked authority the Fourth Amendment is written to prevent. The Supreme Court has consistently held that home deserves the highest level of constitutional protection. Entering a private residence without consent generally requires a judicial warrant. Administrative warrants simply do not meet that standard. They bypass judicial oversight and weaken the constitutional barrier that protects residents from unreasonable searches and seizures. This

items.title: Accessory dwelling units
items.text: Accessory dwelling units. Amending 5.7.3 Accessory Dwelling Units of the Cheyenne Unified Development Code to remove owner-occupancy and adjust parking requirements for Accessory Dwellings. A proposed update to owner-occupancy and parking rules for accessory dwellings. Staff report describes about three ADU applications a year. Proposal would remove the owner-occupancy requirement and allow more flexible parking, including a third driveway stall or on-street parking. Approved on second reading January 26, 2026.

items.title: East Cheyenne annexation
items.text: East Cheyenne annexation. Annexing to the City of Cheyenne various tracts of land completely surrounded by current City limits situate in eastern Cheyenne, generally located south of Storey Boulevard, east of Powderhouse Road, north of Dell Range Boulevard, and west of Ridge Road. Bringing surrounded county tracts in eastern Cheyenne into city limits. Unanimous approval on second reading January 26, 2026.

items.title: Private displays on public land
items.text: Private displays on public property. Creating Chapter 8.72, Private Displays on Public Property, to prohibit the unauthorized use of public property for specified private displays. Proposed rules for unauthorized private displays on public property. First reading referred to the Public Services Committee on January 26, 2026.

items.title: Administrative inspection warrants
items.text: Administrative inspection warrants. Creating Chapter 1.28, Administrative Inspection Warrants, establishing authority for their issuance, and authorizing certain city officials to apply for administrative inspection warrants. Public testimony raised Fourth Amendment and judicial oversight concerns. Postponed to February 9, 2026 rather than adopted at third reading.

items.title: East Cheyenne zoning
items.text: East Cheyenne zoning. Amending the Official Zoning Map of the City of Cheyenne, establishing AG Agricultural and MR Medium-Density Residential classifications for land annexed south of Storey Boulevard, east of Powderhouse Road, north of Dell Range Boulevard, and west of Ridge Road. Companion to the East Cheyenne annexation. Unanimous approval on second reading January 26, 2026.
